title: US Resumes Strikes on Iran, Hitting Larak Island as IRGC Missiles Target US Bases in Jordan
subhead: Washington carried out its first known strike on Iran since late July, bombing IRGC rocket launchers on Larak Island, and Tehran responded with ballistic missiles aimed at US bases in Jordan. The exchange breaks a weeks-long pause and reopens a direct US-Iran military front even as truce talks remain deadlocked.

sections.heading: US-Iran: Strikes Resume, Jordan Front Opens
sections.body:
US Central Command said its forces bombed two IRGC rocket launchers on Larak Island, just offshore from the key port of Bandar Abbas and sitting directly on the Strait of Hormuz, according to the BBC. Iran's Tasnim news agency reported the attack was carried out by drones and that two people were killed and two others injured. It is the first known US strike on Iran since President Donald Trump paused a renewed military campaign in late July.

Hours later, Iranian media carried an IRGC statement saying it had attacked the US bases of King Hussein and al-Azraq in Jordan with ballistic missiles in response, claiming 'heavy damage' to technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities and fighter jet positions, per an AFP translation. Jordan's armed forces said its air defense systems intercepted eight missiles that breached the kingdom's airspace at dawn Monday, according to the state Petra News Agency. IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi called the US attack a 'strategic and fatal mistake' and warned the 'enemy will pay the consequences of this miscalculation in both the economic and military fields.'
sections.whyItMatters: The exchange breaks a roughly month-long pause in direct US-Iran strikes and opens a new front in Jordan, a key US ally hosting American forces. It signals the deadlocked truce talks are sliding back toward open conflict at the world's most critical energy chokepoint.

sections.heading: Washington Tightens the Economic Screw on Tehran
sections.body:
Alongside the military exchange, the US is planning to sanction another Iranian bank to keep economic pressure on Tehran amid the deadlocked truce talks, Al Jazeera reported. The move follows a fresh sanctions campaign announced on 24 August aimed at further isolating Iran and expanding secondary sanctions against its allies, according to the BBC.

Iranian officials and state media have largely dismissed the campaign as a continuation of previous US measures, which they argue followed Washington's military failure in the recent conflict. Iran is currently making tanker traffic pass by Larak Island for checking and reportedly forcing vessels to pay $2m to cross, the BBC noted, underscoring how Tehran continues to monetize its control of the Strait of Hormuz even as the US claims the mines it laid have been cleared.
sections.whyItMatters: The combination of renewed military strikes and stepped-up banking sanctions shows Washington is applying simultaneous military and economic pressure, while Iran's continued tolling of Hormuz traffic keeps the global energy route hostage to the standoff.

sections.heading: Niger Mutiny Puts Russia's Sahel Role to the Test
sections.body:
Niger's military government contained an attempted mutiny that began Saturday at Base 101, a military installation at Diori Hamani International Airport in Niamey, before fighting spread to sites near the presidential palace and the state broadcaster, Al Jazeera reported. State media said dozens of soldiers were killed or arrested, though Reuters said it could not independently verify the figures.

Russia's Africa Corps, the Defense Ministry force that took over much of the Wagner Group's role after Yevgeny Prigozhin's death, was involved in the government's response. Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, said Nigerien authorities requested the force's assistance, and the Associated Press reported Africa Corps provided ground and aerial support to forces loyal to the government. The uprising appears to be the most serious internal challenge to General Abdourahamane Tiani's rule since he seized power in a July 2023 coup.
sections.whyItMatters: Russian forces helping a junta put down a mutiny within its own military marks a deepening of Moscow's security role in the Sahel, where Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso have cut ties with Western partners. It also exposes the fragility of military rule that jihadist violence helped bring to power.

sections.heading: Maduro's First Photos From US Detention Surface
sections.body:
Former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro posted two photographs that appear to show him in a US detention centre, where he has been held since his January abduction by US special forces along with his wife, Cilia Flores, Al Jazeera reported. The pair are held in a facility in Brooklyn, New York, on drug trafficking and firearm possession charges, which they deny. The photos, his first from detention, show him in a grey tracksuit making peace signs and appear to have been taken on June 25.

The message was published two days after Maduro's successor, interim President Delcy Rodriguez, announced a 'historic' oil agreement allowing the US to operate oil fields in Venezuela. Maduro's trial and that of his wife is due to begin on 1 June 2027, a federal court in New York announced in late July.
sections.whyItMatters: The timing of Maduro's first public images, days after Washington struck an oil deal with his successor, highlights the awkward reality of the US doing business with a government whose former leader it is prosecuting — a dynamic that will shape Venezuela's recovery and US energy policy.

sections.heading: Ferry Capsizes Off Northern Cyprus, Eight Dead
sections.body:
At least eight people died and more than a dozen remained missing after a passenger ferry capsized off northern Cyprus, the head of the Turkish administration there said, according to the BBC. The privately owned Filo Jet vessel was carrying 259 passengers and eight crew when it began taking on water after departing the coastal town of Kyrenia. The ship's captain and seven crew members have been detained as part of an investigation.

Prime Minister Unal Ustel said the boat was hit by two waves before it capsized, and Turkish authorities joined a search and rescue operation. The vessel sails under the flag of Turkey, and President Recep Tayyip Erdogan sent condolences to Turkish Cypriots. The TRNC, recognised only by Turkey, controls the northern third of the island, which has been divided since 1974.
sections.whyItMatters: The disaster is a humanitarian and maritime-safety event in the eastern Mediterranean involving Turkey and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, and it will likely strain the already contested politics of the divided island as an investigation into the sinking begins.

bottomLine: The day's defining development is the resumption of direct US-Iran military strikes — Washington hit IRGC launchers on Larak Island and Tehran answered with ballistic missiles aimed at US bases in Jordan — breaking a month-long pause and reopening a front at the Strait of Hormuz even as truce talks stay deadlocked. Alongside it, Russia's Africa Corps helped Niger's junta crush a mutiny, deepening Moscow's grip on the Sahel, while Maduro's first photos from US detention surfaced days after Washington struck an oil deal with his successor. The Iran escalation, in particular, raises the risk that the world's most critical energy chokepoint and the wider Gulf standoff slide back toward open conflict.
